item.title: Why the Russian Exclave of Kaliningrad Is at the Center of a NATO Row
item.description: Amid escalating tensions, the strategically important exclave nestled between Lithuania and Poland is a potential flashpoint with NATO.

media:content.media:description: A member of the Lithuanian Armed Forces rides an all terrain vehicle with a member of Lithuanian State Border Guard Service as they monitor the Lithuanian border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Oct. 26, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea has the potential to become a flashpoint with NATO as recent maritime security incidents between Russia and Ukraine bring renewed attention to the territory nestled between two NATO members.

Moscow on Monday announced the allocation of approximately 47 billion rubles (around $572 million) toward the construction of two railway ferries between the Russian mainland and Kaliningrad, which sits between Poland and Lithuania. 

Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the aim is “to ensure the region has an uninterrupted supply of essential goods and raw materials.” 

Russia relies heavily upon the ice-free port of Kaliningrad, especially since 2022, when Lithuania restricted the transit of certain Russian goods in line with E.U. sanctions put in place following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In 2025, around 52% of goods in and out of the territory were transported via sea, compared to just 8% via the same route in 2021, according to data shared by officials belonging to Rosmorport, a Russian state-owned port operator.

The planned railway ferries come amid concerns from Russia that NATO could use its Baltic presence to isolate Kaliningrad, presenting Moscow with a potential military challenge as the exclave is considered to be a vital asset. According to quotes carried by Russian state media, Mishustin said the investment was needed due to “the illegal actions of certain countries, disruptions to supply chains, and attempts at transport blockades [that] hinder the operations of businesses located there.” He did not specify which countries or specific actions he was referring to. TIME has reached out to Mishustin’s office for further comment. 

The news came shortly after Sparta II, a Russian cargo vessel that was bound for Kaliningrad, was struck in the Gulf of Finland on Nov. 21. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was responsible for the assault, arguing that Sparta II had been carrying military supplies and was therefore a credible target.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov criticized the attack as an example of a “dangerous trend of expanding terrorist activity in the Baltic region.” 

Russia is aiming for the ferries to go into operation in 2030, traveling between the ports of Ust-Luga in Russia's Leningrad region and Baltiysk in Kaliningrad. 

The investment plan “shows that Russia thinks [Kaliningrad] is potentially a long-term vulnerability,” says Natia Seskuria, head of the Russia, Eurasia, and Black Sea security programme at the Royal United Services Institute think tank. “Given the current security environment, and as [Russia] does not expect that this will necessarily ease, they're preparing for a long-term scenario.”

On the same day the Russian vessel was struck in the Baltic Sea, Kaliningrad’s governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said that a drone alert had been activated near the Lithuanian border. He claimed it was triggered by a “suspicious object coming from the direction of Lithuania.”  Kęstutis Budrys, Lithuania’s Foreign Minister, staunchly rejected claims his country was involved in the incident. “The Republic of Lithuania has never authorized the use of its airspace for attacks against targets in the Russian Federation, including in the present case,” he said.

“NATO already perceives Kaliningrad as a potential flashpoint,” says Seskuria, arguing that these recent incidents will likely have raised pre-existing concerns. 

In late September, Russia sent a document to NATO warning it would be open to resorting to the use of nuclear weaponry if NATO attempted to isolate Kaliningrad. 

Russian embassies in European countries including Ireland, the U.K., and Belgium issued statements accusing NATO of escalating tensions by conducting military exercises and planning scenarios “specifically aimed at the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad at the coast of the Baltic Sea.”

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told reporters on Sept. 30 that NATO had been “clear” in its response to Russia. “Basically what we said is, ‘Hey, listen, we are [a] defensive alliance, and stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful. And particularly stop the war in Ukraine, which is [an] unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,’” he said. Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova later dismissed NATO’s concerns, asserting that “ordinary Europeans are being scared with apocalyptic scenarios” in reference to the talk of nuclear threats.

The Baltic region has become particularly important within the context of NATO-Russia relations, with Finland and Sweden, both of which border the body of water, becoming members of the alliance in 2023 and 2024 respectively. 

With Kaliningrad proving to be a long-standing point of tension for NATO and its allies, here’s what to know about the strategically-important Russian exclave. 

What and where is Kaliningrad?

The Russian exclave of Kaliningrad is sandwiched between NATO countries Poland and Lithuania.

Kaliningrad refers to both the exclave as a whole, an area that spans around 5,830 square miles, and the territory’s largest city.

The city of Kaliningrad is around 400 miles away from Russia’s main landmass.

As of June 2025, the region’s total population stands at just over 1 million, around half of which live in the city of Kaliningrad. 

What is the history of Kaliningrad?

It was formerly part of Germany’s East Prussia region. Following World War II, part of East Prussia was ceded to the Soviet Union, with the rest given to Poland in alignment with the Potsdam Agreement signed by Allies in August 1945. 

The city of Koenigsberg was subsequently renamed Kaliningrad in honor of Mikhail Kalinin, who had served as the head of state for the Soviet Union. 

Why is Kaliningrad strategically significant?

Due to its positioning deeper within Europe and its access to the Baltic Sea, Kaliningrad has become a key stronghold for Russia.

“Russia has always seen Kaliningrad as a launching point for potential aggression against Europe, and as they have moved to a further threatening posture against NATO member states, Kaliningrad is of course important to support that,” says Mason Clark, director of the Defense of Europe Project at the Institute for the Study of War.

Moscow has therefore bolstered the territory with military capabilities, particularly in recent years. “Russia has S-300 and S-400 air defense systems based there, as well as, most importantly, Iskander-M systems, which are nuclear capable,” says Seskuria.

Kaliningrad’s ice-free port is also vital for Russia’s naval operations in the region, because it means "vessels can transit in and out of the port at all times of year,” Clark notes.

“While Kaliningrad gives Moscow a base from which it can directly threaten Baltic states and Eastern Europe in general, its geography also makes it vulnerable,” says Seskuria. “Russia has always stressed on heavily fortifying and militarizing this exclave.”

Tensions between Russia and NATO members over Kaliningrad

Escalating tensions came to the forefront in May when Lithuania's Foreign Minister Budrys said NATO must have a firm response to any Russian aggression and would have to show Moscow it was ​capable of penetrating Kaliningrad.

In an interview with a Swiss newspaper, Budrys said: "We have to show the Russians that ⁠we’re capable of penetrating the small fortress they’ve built in Kaliningrad. NATO has the capability, ​if necessary, to raze Russian air defenses and missile bases there to the ground." Peskov responded by saying the statement verged "on insanity" and insisted it was a sign that the Baltic states exhibit "anti-Russian" sentiments.

In September, Russia sent NATO a document indicating it would be open to a potential nuclear response if the alliance attempted ​to cut off Kaliningrad.

Amid a broader conversation about security, Estonia’s Foreign Affairs Minister Margus Tsahkna warned that NATO could close the Baltic Sea “within hours,” cutting the Russian economy’s maritime “lifeline” via the Gulf of Finland if Putin were to carry out any attack that triggers NATO's Article 5 clause.

Should a conflict break out between Russia and the alliance, Moscow would likely look to cut off Baltic nations from the rest of NATO by seizing the Suwalki corridor, a 40-mile stretch of the Poland-Lithuania border flanked by Kaliningrad and Belarus, Russia’s regional ally, experts tell TIME.

“The Russian military would [potentially] try to close the Suwalki corridor between Kaliningrad and Belarus in order to prevent NATO from being able to reinforce the Baltic states by land,” says Clark, emphasizing that this would be a "maximalist scenario” and a full-scale war is highly unlikely at the moment.

item.title: Denis Villeneuve on Drastic Changes in His Dune: Part 3 Movie: ‘When You Adapt, You Kill’
item.description: The director discusses why he changed Chani, the Bond casting process, and his movie coinciding with the release of the latest Avengers installment

media:content.media:description: Timothée Chalamet with director Denis Villeneuve on the set of Dune: Part Three

item.content:encoded:
Denis Villeneuve is finally done wandering the desert. The writer-director has spent nearly a decade adapting Frank Herbert’s Dune and Dune Messiah, the saga of Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet), a young duke stranded on the desert planet of Arrakis, the only source of the universe’s most precious commodity, spice. Embraced as a messiah by the native Fremen thanks to the machinations of a religious order called the Bene Gesserit, Paul ends Dune: Part Two by avenging his father, seizing the throne, and launching a war. At the beginning of Dune: Part Three, which opens Dec. 18, billions have died in his name, and Paul faces a conspiracy that includes his wife, Princess Irulan (Florence Pugh), and Chani (Zendaya), the estranged Fremen mother of his children. The director of previous hits including Sicario, Arrival, and Blade Runner 2049 spoke with TIME about radical adaptation choices in his trilogy’s final chapter and his plans for his next project, a James Bond film, whose new star, Robert Pattinson, was announced a week after our conversation.

Fans of Dune Messiah have called the book unadaptable. 

The book is a chamber piece. People are meeting in rooms talking. It’s a complex, paranoid book. It’s also a kind of depressing book that was not welcomed by Dune readers. The first book is more like an elegy of a hero. And Herbert felt that he was missing the mark because he wanted to create a warning against messianic figures. He felt he needed to correct the trajectory of the story. So yes, it was a big challenge to make this adaptation. The opening battle, which is about 15 minutes in the movie, is one sentence in the book. It’s such a free adaptation that I felt it would have been dishonest to call the movie Dune Messiah. That’s why it’s called Dune: Part Three.

The biggest departure is Paul’s love interest, Chani. In the books, she stays loyal to him even after he marries the emperor’s daughter and becomes this messianic figure. In your movie, Paul and Chani have children together, but she later fights against Paul’s regime. Why the change?

It all started with the adaptation for Dune: Part Two. I was facing the challenge of trying to embrace Herbert’s idea to create a story that would be a warning, not a celebration. At the end of the first book, Paul wins the battle, marries a princess, still gets Chani, and becomes emperor. When you read the book, you’re like, this is a celebration of a hero. I had the idea to make Chani more of a critic regarding the idea of religious colonization. It’s not in the book, the idea that the older generations are contaminated by the beliefs of the Bene Gesserit, by the colonialist religious poison. And the new generation doesn’t believe in the messiah. They want Fremen to be freed by the Fremen themselves. I thought it was a dynamic idea, Chani being the representation of this.

In the third movie, Chani is still a critic of the choices Paul has made. She believes the Fremen should free themselves. She doesn’t want to harm Paul, but she does want to harm his regime. I would have loved to have taken Frank Herbert for a coffee about these ideas because I think he could have liked them. In his book, Chani is there to give Paul foot massages. It’s a character that has not a lot of firepower.

Did you worry about upsetting book purists?

When you adapt, you kill. It is not the book. It is my movie inspired by the book, with tremendous respect. My three movies embrace the Bene Gesserit angle because that is what I thought was most inspiring, relevant, and cinematic. But you could make an entire Dune adaptation focused on the idea that humans have fought AI and banned machines. Those ideas aren’t in my movies because it’s too much. You have to make choices. That’s the beauty of adaptation.

There is a big time jump between Part Two and Part Three. Paul and Chani have teenage children now. You originally planned to take a long break between those films. What changed?

I did [Part One and Part Two] back to back, without a single day break between. They were not easy births. I’m not complaining. I’m just explaining that I said to myself while filming Part Two, the only way to get out of this alive is to take a break. I’m going to the forest to hide for many months. And I did. The problem is that after two weeks, I got bored. My wife asked me, “What are you doing?” And I said, “I’m writing Part Three.” I was waking up at night with cinematic images. I was working on another project, but every image coming to my mind was from Dune Messiah.

What images?

The final one of Paul. It’s a moment that haunted me all these years, and I think I did the trilogy to make that image.

One that has stuck with me from the movie is the opening battle. Was there a particular cinematic touchpoint?

It’s difficult to see men coming out of a troop transport being decimated without thinking of Saving Private Ryan. It’s obvious. I knew I was stepping into delicate territory because that is one of the most celebrated cinematic sequences of the past 30 years. But I felt it was what the scene needed. I have been dreaming about shooting a landing on the beaches of Normandy since I was a kid.

Another was Florence Pugh, covered in clay, walking through the maze to Paul. I don’t believe that was in the book. Where did that come from?

At the beginning of Part Three, Paul is unable to find a peaceful way out of the violence. He becomes more and more paranoid and isolated. We’re not sure if he’s lost contact with reality. How do you express that? Princess Irulan has to meet her own husband she hasn’t seen in years. How does he live? How can he protect himself from the assassination attempts? We created a space as if Irulan is walking into the subconscious space of Paul, like the Greek story of Theseus and the Minotaur, where Theseus walks into the labyrinth in order to kill the monster. Irulan won’t kill Paul, but this idea of her going into that maze to neutralize the source of evil was inspiring.

You’ve called this your most personal film in a long time. How so?

One of the ideas is what kind of world Paul and Chani are trying to leave their children. And what happens to this heritage when you are going through a divorce? That’s a question that anyone who has a broken family understands. It’s vivid and profound to me. 

Dune: Part Three premieres the same weekend as Avengers: Doomsday. How are you feeling about that?

Listen, I will be honest. The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us. Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy. The third time, I said to myself, “Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release.” Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth.

So I was deeply disappointed. But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.

After living within Dune for so long, how difficult is it to transition to a different world for James Bond?

I don’t sleep a lot right now because it’s like I have electricity in my veins thinking about this new project. It is so different. I spent 10 years of my life in the sun talking about a specific color palette, thinking about ways to embrace natural light. I adore being on Arrakis, but I think it’s healthy to step away.

Are there things you feel are essential to Bond that need to be maintained?

I don’t want to talk too much about Bond because it’s still in the oven cooking. This stage of the process is my favorite part because everything is possible.

I will say: I love traditions. I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache. I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today. I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film. Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure.

We are speaking ahead of the much-anticipated casting announcement. Are you aware that people were placing bets on Polymarket?

I read nothing about that. My responsibility is to make the best casting and create the best story for that cast. I cannot listen to the rumors. No matter what we do, we will never please everybody.

When Daniel Craig was cast, it was a sh-tstorm. He was blond. He was short. He was not seen as an action hero. Yet when we talk about James Bond today it is because of Daniel Craig’s extraordinary interpretation. And that was a different environment in 2006 before social media. I expect a hurricane when we bring our choice to the world. Some people will be happy. Some will be mad. I can do nothing about that. At the end of the day, the truth will be on the screen. Then they will be able to judge.

item.title: How to Have a More Sustainable Black Friday, According to Experts
item.description: If you plan to shop, here's how to help your wallet—and the planet.

media:content.media:description: Black Friday signage displayed in a retail window on Oxford Street on Nov. 23, 2026 in London, England.

item.content:encoded:
Black Friday is here—holding the promise of good deals and the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season. 

But if you plan to shop the sales, take the time to think about what you really need—and what you plan to give. Americans spent $10 billion dollars on unwanted gifts in 2024. And last year, 65% of consumers reported returning a holiday gift, while 54% admitted to regifting an unwanted item. So, being more intentional about your holiday shopping can benefit both your wallet and the planet. 

“We are in an era right now where things are very expensive, and so when we're talking about affordability and Black Friday, thinking about what's really going to serve us and make us happy is a great way of thinking about sustainability too,” says Shelie Miller co-director of the Center for Sustainable Systems at the University of Michigan. “Being thoughtful about what's happening to our bank accounts as well as the overall amount of stuff we're buying can be very helpful as far as guiding us to a better path forward.” 

We spoke with experts about how best to avoid overconsumption and shop with sustainability in mind this Black Friday. 

Plan your shopping—and stick to the list

Before you shop, create a list of what you’re looking for to avoid any unwanted impulse purchases. “Having a list and sticking to it can be helpful for curbing some of those impulsive consumptions when that impulsivity is sky high,” says Karen Winterich, professor of marketing at Penn State University. 

When you’re shopping, think twice before jumping on any deals for items that weren’t on your list. “We often get sucked into buying because it feels like a good deal,” says Winterich. “It makes us feel good to get that deal, and then later we may actually feel regret. Like, ‘I got a good deal, but did I even need to buy in the first place?’”

To avoid feeling any regret, focus on how much you’re spending rather than how much you’re saving. “Even if we're saving a lot, we're still spending,” says Winterich. “If it's 90% off, but I don't need it, I'm not going to use it. Don't buy it.”

Be intentional with your gifts

If you’re buying gifts for the holiday season, take some time to think about the person you’re shopping for before you swipe your card. 

“If you're buying for someone else, pause and think about the person and if [the gift] is something they would really want and enjoy and use, or if you’re buying it to check the box, and say, ‘I got them a gift,’” says Winterich. 

If you know your friend has a cupboard full of coffee mugs, consider getting them locally roasted coffee beans or treating them to a coffee instead of buying them another mug. 

Consider gifting something people can consume—especially if you’re buying for someone you don’t know very well, like an office Secret Santa or a new neighbor. 

“Maybe that’s a loaf of local bread or something you make yourself with a locally made jam, or it could be some hot chocolate mix with a special treat attached to it,” says Winterich. “Something that's consumable and not necessarily made from plastics and shipped overseas, but a little bit more locally made, that they're going to consume and not have sitting around or donating. [It conveys] ‘I'm still thinking of you, I'm still giving you a gift, but it's not stuff that is going to sit there that you’re not going to enjoy and appreciate.”

Consider your footprint

Individual actions may not seem like much, but their impact can add up. Every year, people in the United States throw out more than 34 billion lbs of used textiles—roughly 100 lbs of textile waste per person each year—while global electronic waste continues to climb. 

If you’re buying an item online, see if you can pick it up at the store. Last mile delivery, the final step before a product reaches your doorstop, is responsible for roughly half of a delivery’s total emissions. “If you know you're already going to be going to the store, maybe you could just pick out one day in the week and say I'm going to hit these couple stores up where I have items to pick up at, rather than having that individual last mile delivery,” says Winterich. 

Consider shopping for quality rather than quantity—and be mindful of what you might already have at home. “A lot of times with impulse buys we're trying to get as much stuff for as little money as possible,” says Miller. “When we're talking about sustainability, we want people to use items for a long time to get their best environmental value.”

“Everything that we buy had [manufacturing and shipping] impacts that were many times bigger than the product itself,” continues Miller. “So [thinking] maybe that stocking stuffer isn't really going to bring joy, and it's just going to affect my pocketbook. That actually has some environmental [benefits] to it.”

item.title: Why You Should Train to Be Ethically Fit
item.description: "We can become and stay ethically fit by cultivating ethical strength and agility," write David W. Miller with Susan Richardson.
item.content:encoded:
Think of great athletes; they are fit in a way that relies on years of training and practice. An accomplished track star did not suddenly decide to run the four-minute mile one morning and have all the skills, strength, and endurance to do it. Elite tennis players prepare for and anticipate mid-game scenarios and know just what shot to draw on because they’ve practiced it thousands of times. Or think of great musicians who are fit because they’ve practiced scales, arpeggios, and studies for years before they perform a challenging work. A brilliant cellist did not suddenly decide to play the Bach cello suites one morning and have it artfully under her fingers immediately. They have cultivated their ability by keeping the skills going all along. In each case, they developed and practiced their skills—their fitness or wellness, so to speak—over time so they would be ready when they’re playing in pressure-packed moments under the bright lights. 

Our research and experience convince us that we can become and stay ethically fit by cultivating ethical strength and agility so that, when the moment comes, the muscle patterns and range of motion we need are there. The question for many then becomes how to get those muscles and then keep them in shape. You could certainly delve into the great classical schools of ethics, reading in-depth tomes by thinkers past and present. You could probe the great ancient spiritual and religious traditions for their wisdom on the human struggle with right and wrong and the practices that can help. You could read policies and laws related to ethics, which would easily take up multiple volumes (and lots of time). Or you might look to recent psychological and neurological studies on the way our brains work and why, realizing the “right” thing may be trickier than we think. These are all great things to do… if you have the time and the bandwidth. But for many of us, life’s demands mean that instead, we need to harvest the core ideas from all these traditions and craft an intellectually robust, informed, and practical set of ethical tools while also cultivating the strength to wield them. 

You can move from simply having knowledge—the ethical exercises—to having wisdom, a reflective way of looking at decisions in your life and indeed at yourself. I hope that as you think about what success looks like in your life, and what you want it to look like in the future, such wisdom will be part of it. 

Life is all about decisions, in which we act out—and often find out—who we are. There are a range of ways to think about how ethics works in our lives. But given how decisions both draw on who we’ve been and shape who we’re becoming, we’ll focus here on decision-making as an elevated moment in the ethical landscape of our lives. How we want to see ourselves as behaving and how we actually behave in the moment, or our “lived ethic,” can all too easily be two different things. As you reflect honestly on your recent decisions, what is your own lived ethic? What is mine? And how can it be wiser and more informed for the sake of your future self and those you care about? 

Experiences from the past, things in the moment that can throw us off balance, and an unrealistic sense of the future can make a sound ethical decision difficult to discern. What we need are the tools and practices for effectively tackling ethical decisions, particularly when the dilemma is in the ethical gray zone or, worse, disguised and unrecognizable until it is too late. 

Ethics is not simply about laws and compliance. Rather, it’s also about character (yours) and culture (your organization’s). This is not to take away from compliance officers and departments; indeed, hopefully, it will affirm their importance as one place in the larger picture. Compliance departments and guidelines are necessary but not sufficient. They tend to look backward, focused on catching those who’ve violated laws and regulations, whereas ethics understood as character and culture is focused on avoiding future mistakes. Law, codes, and policy are an important place to begin, but we need to use other ethical perspectives as well. Similarly, ethics is not merely about telling people to be “good” or “moral,” an approach that can be misleading and unhelpful. First, telling someone just to “be moral” can put inordinate pressure on them without giving them the tools they need to fulfill the expectation. And telling people to be good can also be interpreted in too many ways. More helpful is an approach that helps you identify ethical problems as such and know your own ethical sources and tools for making an ethical decision. Such an approach helps you better imagine possible outcomes, either positive or negative, and see yourself working through them. 

But if ethics isn’t only about compliance or the admonition to be good, then what else is it? My view is that it also gathers the two critical pieces of character and culture, which in turn invite deeper questions. 

What shapes and sustains your individual character or the corporate culture of the business or organization you’re a part of? What role (if any) do religious or spiritual traditions play in either one? For many, their faith tradition—even if they move away from the doctrinal claims or practices—remains influential, if not central, to their ethical grounding and sense of societal responsibility. What other sources or reality checks do you use in ethical decision-making—a mentor, for instance, or a close family member you check in with? How carefully do you track and trust your intuition and gut instinct? 

Your lived ethic is the behavior and values you personally bring into an ethical decision. But the fact is you’re never there alone. You are in an ethical field, which can be compared with a playing field in sports. That field comprises the context in which your personal ethics and decision-making is taking place, including external factors, organizational ethics, and the ethics of other people. For ethical decisions, we are rarely solo actors.

item.title: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
item.description: The bitter partisan fight to redraw congressional maps may be dying down—at least for now.

media:content.media:description: Voting booths at a polling location inside Wayne Community College - Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Nov. 1, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Republicans and Democrats in several states engaged in a bitter fight to redraw congressional maps in their parties’ favor leading up to this year’s midterms. But in the aftermath of the blue wave that swept across the country, that conflict may be dying down—at least for now.

Typically, maps are redrawn after the results of the U.S. census are released each decade, in order to account for population and demographic changes. Last year, however, President Donald Trump urged members of his party to redistrict mid-cycle ahead of the 2026 election as the GOP vied to hold onto its narrow House majority. Several Republican-led states moved to do so in the ensuing months, while Democratic leaders in other states responded with their own redistricting efforts, with varying degrees of success. 

The sweeping Democratic victories in the midterms, though, could mark a shift in the redistricting battle, political experts tell TIME.

Read More: Are Democrats’ Stunning Midterm Upsets in Deep-Red States a Blip—or Is Their Map Expanding?

Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, says that Republicans may be more reluctant to push for redistricting mid-cycle going forward, given that their efforts failed to counteract the blue wave in this year’s election. 

In states like Texas, North Carolina, Ohio, Alabama, and Florida, Democratic candidates came out on top in multiple districts that had been redrawn to benefit Republicans—which political experts have largely attributed to the fact that, despite redistricting efforts, Republicans were still facing a challenging political climate at a time when Trump’s approval rating was at a historic low.

“In recent years, Democrats have been reluctant to engage in mid-cycle redistricting. Republicans have been more willing to do that, and Democrats have followed suit in response in order to counteract some of the districts created by Republicans to advantage themselves,” Panagopoulos says. 

“But as 2026 showed us, those efforts often amount to very little and can even backfire, so I think both parties right now are cautious about any mid-cycle redistricting efforts, and 2026 suggests that even if districts are very heavily gerrymandered to advantage one party or the other, there are no guarantees that those parties will win,” he continues.

Mark Jones, a professor of political science at Rice University, says that, for Republicans, “pretty much anything that they could have done, they already did.” And he says that even if there are states where additional redistricting could in theory help make maps even more favorable for Republicans, GOP lawmakers will now face a challenging time pushing such legislation through if their power in the state governments was reduced—for instance, in Texas, where Democrats gained control of the state House and the governorship.

Meanwhile, the Democrats who were advocating for redistricting in recent months were doing so as “defensive measures,” says Alvin Tillery, the director of Northwestern University’s Center for the Study of Democratic Governance and a Democratic pollster and consultant. And Jones says that, with the party’s sizable victories in this year’s midterms, “the sense of urgency” to redistrict “is no longer there.” 

It’s possible, Jones says, that some “unfinished business” may continue—for instance, Virginians passed a redistricting ballot measure in April, but the state Supreme Court prevented the newly drawn maps from taking effect; Jones says that Democrats could try to take up that effort again. 

But generally speaking, “I don’t think we’re going to see the gerrymander armed race in 2027 that we saw in 2025,” Jones says. If some of those efforts do proceed, he says, “I think it’s going to be at the margins.”

“The Democratic Party reluctantly engaged in mid-decade redistricting only after Donald Trump and Republicans drew first blood, and given the size of the victory and the lesser the sense of urgency and need to bolster the number of seats that are safely Democratic, I think we’re going to see Democrats try to return to the norms that have governed U.S. politics in the modern era,” Jones says.

That doesn’t mean that partisan gerrymandering has come to an end, experts point out. The next redistricting cycle will take place after the 2030 census, and Panagopoulos says, “When it’s a redistricting cycle, both parties engage to the extent that they can in partisan gerrymandering.” And Democrats, he says, “will remain better positioned to engage in pro-Democratic redistricting in part because of the gains that they made in state legislatures and governorships across the country.”

“I don’t think redistricting is high on any party’s agenda at the moment,” Panagopoulos says. But, he continues, “Things will clearly shift in the aftermath of the 2030 survey, and what will be more important is what the partisan makeup of states and state legislatures looks like at that time.”

item.title: Trump Accuses His Own Government of Falsifying Economic Data
item.description: In his Thanksgiving message on social media, Trump called for an investigation into a routine revision to economic data, calling it a “massive, and purposeful, error.”

media:content.media:description: President Donald Trump participates in a Thanksgiving call with U.S. service members from Palm Beach, Fla., Nov. 26, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has accused his own government of deliberately falsifying economic data before the midterm elections in which Republicans saw sweeping losses.

“I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late,” Trump posted on Truth Social Thursday. “A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated.” His holiday post also made jabs at the “Radical Far Left,” immigrants, and “Reporters and Citizens” who have criticized his White House ballroom project.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) revised its estimate of third-quarter annualised growth to 4.3%, up from the advance estimate of 3.4% published on Oct. 29. Annualized growth tracks how much the economy would grow over a year if it kept growing at that quarter’s pace. The updated figures, which were published according to a prescheduled calendar, reflect an increase from 2.2% in the second quarter.

In another post on Thursday, Trump called the revision a “massive, and purposeful, error.”

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” he posted. He did not provide evidence of manipulation.

TIME has reached out to the Commerce Department and BEA for comment.

It’s not the first time that Trump has sought to undermine economic data that didn’t reflect his claims of economic prosperity. In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump frequently claimed the U.S. economy was experiencing a major boom, citing stock market highs and pointing to his tariffs as enriching the country. When the advance estimate was published in October, the White House called it “the strongest pace in a year” and evidence of “an economy that continues to outperform the so-called ‘experts.’” Voters, however, appeared to see things differently: 76% said economic conditions were “not so good” or “poor,” according to the AP Voter Poll, and two-thirds said they believed Trump’s policies had driven up inflation. Nine in 10 midterm voters said the cost of living was a major factor in their vote.

Reports on Wednesday showed a mixed picture of the economy. The BEA raised its estimate of growth in consumer spending and private fixed investment combined, pointing to stronger economic growth in the third quarter. At the same time, a separate BEA report showed that the personal consumption expenditures price index, a key measure of inflation, rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier. New York Fed analysts also estimated last month that Trump’s tariffs had added 2.9 percentage points to year-over-year inflation for consumer goods by February. Without tariffs, the researchers said, goods prices would have fallen slightly.

Trump’s history of selectively undermining economic data

Even before he became President, Trump questioned the integrity of economic statistics. “It’s a false economy that we’re living in,” Trump, who was then the GOP frontrunner, told CBS’ Face the Nation in 2015, before launching into a diatribe against the unemployment rate. 

On the campaign trail, he called the job numbers “phony” and a “joke.” In February 2016, he falsely stated the unemployment rate was as high as 35% and that he “heard” it even reached 42%, while official figures showed the figure hovered near 5%. Later that year, without evidence, he called the 5% unemployment rate “one of the biggest hoaxes in modern politics.”

But after his first inauguration, Trump slightly changed his tune on economic figures. In March 2017, then-Press Secretary Sean Spicer was asked about a released jobs report, to which he responded: “I talked to the President prior to this, and he said to quote him very clearly — ‘They may have been phony in the past, but it’s very real now.’” At a round table in July that year, Trump acknowledged having dismissed unemployment figures before, adding: “now I accept those numbers very proudly.”

The President has also accused the U.S. press, without evidence, of manipulating some figures to deny his achievements. In 2019, Trump accused the press of revising a 3.1% economic growth figure downward to 2.9%, when reporters were citing figures from Trump’s own Commerce Department.

In July 2022, while out of office and speaking in Arizona, Trump slammed a 40-year record-high inflation rate of 9.1% under the Joe Biden Administration, and he claimed, without substantiation, that the actual number was much higher. “Biden created the worst inflation in 47 years,” Trump said.

In August 2024, the Biden Administration’s Bureau of Labor Statistics preliminarily revised down the benchmark payroll growth for the year ending in March by 818,000 jobs. Trump called it a “massive scandal,” arguing that it wasn’t a revision but “a total lie,” and accused the Biden Administration of “fraudulently manipulating job statistics to hide the true extent of the economic ruin that they’ve inflicted on America.” 

In August 2025, after Trump returned to the White House, he fired BLS commissioner Erika McEntarfer, a Biden appointee, for allegedly manipulating job figures to reflect poorly on his Administration. “Today’s Jobs Numbers were RIGGED to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad,” the President posted on Truth Social at the time. The White House also published what it said was a “lengthy history of inaccuracies and incompetence,” citing revisions.

Trump’s own former BLS commissioner William Beach and other federal statistical experts have said claims of manipulation have no merit and undermine the credibility of economic statistics. 

How the numbers are calculated—and revised

The BEA routinely revises its estimates of annualized growth and other economic data. The agency bases its advance estimate on two or three months of available source data and makes assumptions where data is still missing or preliminary. When new data or survey results become available, the agency revises its figures to be more accurate.

Those updates happen on a prescheduled basis. The advance estimate typically comes out around a month after the quarter ends, the second estimate about two months after, and the third estimate around three months after. For the third quarter of 2026, the BEA released the advance estimate on Oct. 29 and the second estimate Nov. 25, with the third scheduled for Dec. 23. The White House budget office published the calendar for all three estimates in September 2025. While federal policy allows for schedule changes in certain circumstances, such as the 2025 government shutdown, in this case, contrary to Trump’s assertion that the second estimate was “three weeks late,” the estimates came out on time.

Wednesday’s revision happened because revised software price and retail sales data pushed up estimates of software investment and goods spending, while new Census survey data lowered the estimate of health care spending, the agency said. The agency cited new and revised Energy Department data for consumer spending on gas as pushing up overall goods spending. The 0.9-percentage-point revision was bigger than the BEA’s historical average of 0.5 percentage points difference between a first and second estimate.

There are broader pressures that can make early economic estimates less precise. A Nov. 17 report from the American Statistical Association (ASA) found that response rates declined from 2016 to 2025 in eight of the 10 surveys of businesses and prices it reviewed. Fewer responses can reduce precision and force agencies to rely more heavily on estimates for missing data. Falling participation can also lead to bias based on which households or businesses respond and which don’t. Brookings analysts suggested in April that people may be difficult to contact, reluctant to respond because they are busy, or concerned about keeping their data private.

“A falling response rate does not automatically mean that a survey’s estimates are inaccurate. It increases the risk that estimates do not remain as accurate and representative as they have been in the past,” the ASA said.

The BEA has also faced staffing cuts under the Trump Administration. Its workforce shrank by around 21% from 473 employees at the end of fiscal 2024 to 374 by July 2026, according to federal personnel data compiled by the ASA. The ASA also found that the BEA’s fiscal 2026 budget fell around 8% from the previous year after adjusting for inflation. The association warned that staffing losses and funding constraints threaten the timeliness, quality, and availability of federal statistics.

The agency, however, did not name these pressures in its explanation for Wednesday’s revision.

Without responding to Trump’s allegation of purposeful error, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick praised the BEA’s revised estimate as evidence that “The American Economy under The Trump Administration is doing BETTER than every expert estimated!”

“This Thanksgiving, I am thankful to be a part of President Trump's administration, not only for the extraordinary honor of serving the American people, but because I love this Country so much, I know how much better off we are today than we were two years ago, and I know the incredible heights we can reach in the years ahead,” Lutnick posted on X. “4.3% Growth—Happy Thanksgiving!!”

item.title: Trump Urges Putin to ‘Pull Back’ Military Aggression in Europe
item.description: The U.S. President expressed hope that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine "quickly" to avoid expansion of the war.

media:content.media:description: Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Alaska on Aug. 15, 2025.

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump on Thursday said he would like to see Russian President Vladimir Putin “pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe” in the hope that a deal can be made to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

"During my conversations in ​China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I ⁠spent a lot of time talking about the ​fact that I would like to see President ​Putin pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe,” said Trump, referencing the meetings he had with Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit last week.

Expressing his belief that a deal can be made "quickly," Trump continued: “I really believe this is a strong possibility. Thousands of people are being killed each and every month. A complete bloodbath.”

Trump’s update came a day after he met with NATO chief Mark Rutte at his Mar-a-Lago estate. Trump said he informed Rutte of his conversations with Putin during the meeting, which primarily focused on Ukraine and Iran. In a joint statement issued Wednesday night, Trump and Rutte said the “impactful” sit-down had seen them discuss the “importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible.”

However, Trump strayed somewhat from NATO on Thursday by sharing his own version of the "joint statement" on Truth Social that featured a notable addition.

While the official joint NATO statement called for Russia to avoid any actions that could expand the war, Trump widened that instruction to include Ukraine, writing: "We also talked about, at length, the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."

When approached for comment about the differences in the joint statements, NATO referred TIME to the relevant U.S. authorities. TIME has reached out to the White House.

In Trump's follow-up post that called out Putin more directly, he didn’t specify what he meant by “territories throughout Europe,” but his remarks come amid concerns over the possible expansion of the Russia-Ukraine war. 

A number of recent incidents involving NATO members have sparked fears. Last week, Poland accused Russia of ⁠violating its airspace after two missiles and a drone crashed in its territory. Russia denied violating Poland’s airspace. Estonia also recently accused Russian security services ​of ordering an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defense company. Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the accusation “unfounded,” denying Moscow’s involvement. Tensions escalated further this week when Russia alleged that Estonia was quietly allowing Ukrainian drones to use its airspace to strike northwestern Russia and accused Tallinn of trying to obstruct Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea. Estonia vehemently denied both accusations calling them “baseless,” with Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stressing that the country “has not allowed and will not allow its territory or airspace to be used for drone attacks against Russia from Ukraine.”

U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations resumed earlier this month after a nine-month hiatus, but there is still no clear pathway to ending the current conflict which started in February 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine.

Trump, as of late, has raised eyebrows over his interactions with Putin. On the sidelines of the APEC summit last week, he warmly greeted the Russian leader by referring to him as a “friend.” The remark led to stern criticism from the likes of Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Last month, Trump waived sanctions on Russia to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin in an attempt to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran. The move drew condemnation from European leaders and Republican lawmakers.

Russia-Ukraine war intensifies with no clear end in sight

Russia on Thursday accused Ukraine of attempting to expand the geographical scope of the conflict into the Mediterranean and Baltic seas, after Kyiv claimed responsibility for an attack on a Russian warship stationed at a port in Libya and another strike on a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that the attacks could “cause concern among coastal states and, most likely, within the North Atlantic alliance as a whole,” according to Russian state media.

As tensions escalate, Russia launched fresh strikes on Kyiv overnight into Thursday morning, injuring at least seven people, according to the Ukrainian capital's mayor, Vitali Klitschko. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed carrying out strikes, claiming via a Telegram post that it had targeted Ukrainian military equipment with precision weapons.

Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi added that as part of the overnight attacks two foreign ships carrying more than 100,000 tons of grain had been attacked near Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Odessa. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its forces had struck a dry cargo ship with military equipment.

In two separate strikes, Ukrainian forces hit an oil terminal refinery deep into Russian territory, and an airfield base in southern Russia.

Zelensky on Thursday also said that Russia was planning a major attack on Ukraine’s power grid. 

“According to intelligence, energy facilities and logistics infrastructure, as well as essential services facilities in cities and communities, will once again be the targets. I expect a report from Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry on the results of its communication with our partners regarding the supply of air defenses—interceptors for Patriots and NASAMS [Norwegian Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System] are the key priority,” he said via a social media update. 

Europe ramps up pressure on Russia

Europe this week unveiled a sweeping new sanctions proposal aimed at further isolating Russia economically and increasing pressure on Moscow to end the war.

Leaders of the E.U.’s 27 member states met Thursday in Brussels to discuss the bloc’s long-term budget for 2028-2034 and to address Ukraine’s financial needs for 2027. 

Ahead of the meeting, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told reporters that Europe "cannot afford cuts to defense funding" and instead needs to invest more in its security. "If you look at what Russia is doing on the eastern border, the eastern border needs protecting, it needs investments and money," he said.

Ukraine “probably will face a winter like hell” and so “they must know that Europe has their back, with money and everything we have," he urged.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also insisted that support for Ukraine should continue to be at the forefront of discussions. “We must ensure that Ukraine receives sufficient support in the coming years. That applies both militarily and in humanitarian terms,” he said.

Ukraine and its allies have pushed to secure a European seat at the next round of negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.

"Europe will be represented by five countries plus the European Union and NATO, and America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation in the negotiations is necessary," Zelensky said last week after attending a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin. 

Zelensky has since said that Kyiv is “waiting for the American side to set a date for the next meeting.” TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.

item.title: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
item.description: Beijing warned that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs.

media:content.media:description: U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.

item.content:encoded:
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs, which have reignited global trade tensions.

“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.” 

The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.

China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.

Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”

Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, views the tariff proposals as a pressure point on Southeast Asian economies and their trade relations with the U.S. and China.

She says that many of the region’s economies see a lot of Chinese goods pass through before heading to the U.S. market, with tariffs intended to “make it more difficult for economies like Vietnam to position themselves as collector economies between the U.S. and China,” she tells TIME.

The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.

On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.” 

Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.

Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.

“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”

Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.

Overall, the proposed rates are just “one more complication in the relationship with the U.S.” that global partners have to contend with, adds Demarais.

Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.

Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”

Brazil fights back after being singled out

Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.

“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.

The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year. 

“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.

It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.” 

Democratic lawmaker vows to tackle Trump’s tariffs

The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.

Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement. “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”

However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.

Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

item.title: You Can’t Cast Your Family
item.description: When my husband was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's, we met for Thanksgiving as if nothing had changed. Years later, I learned making a scene is worth it.

media:content.media:description: Chevy Chase in a scene from the 1989 film "Christmas Vacation."

item.content:encoded:
One of the first films I cast was the holiday classic National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation. I was one lucky 27-year-old when my bosses invited me to partner with them and help complete casting the Griswold family.

In those days, we auditioned scores of actors in person. Almost everyone came through our doors to read for their roles, something now mostly done over Zoom or by offer only. In my humble opinion, casting has taken a nosedive because we've lost that intimate experience of sitting face-to-face, listening, observing, and discovering a character together. Sometimes it took several auditions, chemistry reads, callbacks, and director work sessions to get it right. We had to slow down and really see the person sitting across from us.

Every holiday season, when millions of American families gather around their Thanksgiving and Christmas tables, I think about those wacky Griswold family dynamics. The relatives who arrive uninvited. The holiday disasters. The misunderstandings, the arguments, and the love beneath all the madness.

In my husband Charlie's family, Thanksgiving was a beloved tradition. His parents divorced when he was 15, and the family learned to move between households and maintain a certain equilibrium. Everyone found ways to come together, but rarely did anyone dig deeper into what was happening beneath the surface. The family had learned to adapt and to compartmentalize their feelings.

Thanksgiving 2019, in Charlie's hometown of Washington, D.C., should have been different.

Charlie's mom had passed away years earlier, and a couple of months before traveling east, we had told his dad, stepmother, and siblings that Charlie, at just 57, had been diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's disease and was leaving his job as an art director at UCLA Magazine.

But once we arrived, the diagnosis seemed to be swept under the rug. Charlie looked so well. His Alzheimer's was invisible to them.

I remember worrying about a fancy dinner at the Cosmos Club because Charlie needed to wear a tie, and neither of us could quite manage to tie one. A small thing, perhaps, but one of those early signs of struggle.

What his family might have noticed were the changes already taking place in our marriage. Charlie's short temper and his uncertainty about what kind of work he might pursue next. My super-sensitive artist husband had actually been the one to recognize that something was wrong and asked to see a doctor. I had simply hoped his mood would change and that further tests might reveal something else. We were on a kind of autopilot in those early days, and I was just beginning to realize there was little I could do to solve this problem.

As always, I had my camera with me. I filmed the family around the Thanksgiving table, sharing the things they were grateful for. Looking back at that footage now is painful.

Charlie's father, a distinguished writer and scholar who had spent nearly 50 years at a Washington think tank after serving in the White House, beamed with pride at his two sons, his beloved wife, stepchildren, and the grandchildren who made him so happy. He was finishing his final memoir and remained intellectually engaged with the world. Yet his oldest son's Alzheimer's diagnosis never entered the Thanksgiving conversation.

Charlie himself was still hopeful about his next act. He was making art, walking the streets of Los Angeles with his camera, and building a website, walkingnla.com, to document his discoveries. His words were beginning to falter, but his wit, his agency, and his joie de vivre remained intact.

"Everybody gets something," he would say, accepting his diagnosis with a kind of courage and wry humor that I still marvel at.

He certainly wasn't looking for a pity party. He wanted to enjoy his family, and perhaps for a few hours forget what was happening to him. 

But somewhere between respecting Charlie's wishes and avoiding the uncomfortable truth, we all managed to sidestep the elephant at the Thanksgiving table. I was part of that conceit, too.

Perhaps that Thanksgiving we were all too frightened of what we didn't know. Fear of the unknown has a funny way of disguising itself as good manners.

When COVID arrived, our world grew smaller. Uncertain about what either of us could do for work, I decided I needed to make a film, WALK WITH ME. Documenting four years of our lives became my way of coping,  and a way to give Charlie purpose. I convinced my family to participate because our story belonged to millions of other families like ours, and that the film could confront the stigma and shame surrounding Alzheimer's disease. What I hadn't anticipated was that it would also document my own transformation into a caregiver. At the time, caregiving wasn't even in my vocabulary.

I will always be grateful for the quiet conversations we had during that time. Making our documentary meant asking my family to bear witness on camera to some of the most difficult moments of our lives. It took years for all of us to work through what that meant. And it took me even longer to own up to adding "caregiver" to my identity.

Watching that 2019 Thanksgiving footage now, I see a family functioning beautifully on the surface. 

But I wish I had asked the questions we were all avoiding.

What would happen when Charlie could no longer manage everyday tasks? Who would help? How would we pay for that help? What would happen to my work, our marriage, and our independence?

I wish I had understood sooner that living with a progressive disease meant grieving each loss while constantly readjusting and improvising so Charlie could remain in the lane of "normal."

Today, I choose restaurants with quiet tables. In movie theaters, I sit beside him in an aisle seat near the exit in case the film becomes too loud or intense and we need to leave. Before flying, I find out where the family bathrooms are located at the airport. I have to pre-think and map out nearly every adventure because I still want Charlie to be with me, and I still want our lives to feel "normal."

But the truth is, nothing is normal anymore. And I wish I had brought his family and friends into the conversation earlier rather than trying to manage so much of it myself. Perhaps if I'd spoken more openly about my fears, they would have understood sooner how much we needed them. Perhaps they would have prioritized showing up for Charlie, and for me. I can't know that. I was still struggling to understand what was happening myself.

It took me nearly two years to confront Charlie's father and tell him how hurt I was that he continued to speak as though nothing was happening. I suspected he was afraid to acknowledge the changes in his son. What parent wants to imagine losing a child, even gradually, to a disease that steals so much?

Seven years later, Charlie needs help with nearly every activity of daily living. I have become his caregiver, his advocate, his interpreter, and often his compass in a world that has become increasingly difficult for him to navigate.

Our children have had to learn how to remain connected to a father who can no longer communicate as he once did. And I have learned that love, however deep, cannot replace the practical, emotional, and financial support that caregiving requires.

This holiday season, millions of Americans will brave crowded highways and impossible airports to gather with relatives they may not have seen for months.

And somewhere between the turkey, the football games, and the arguments about politics, someone may notice that something feels a little off.

Grandma tells the same story three times. An uncle who was always the life of the party becomes irritated when the conversation gets too loud. Mom, who once managed the entire holiday dinner, now seems overwhelmed by the simplest preparations.

It's easy to dismiss these changes as aging, stress, exhaustion, or eccentricity. Sometimes that's exactly what they are. Not every forgotten word or strange behavior signals dementia. But sometimes something more serious is happening, and the holiday table may be the first place everyone has an opportunity to see it.

This holiday season, perhaps the greatest gift we can give the people we love is our attention. Put down the phone. Listen. Observe. Ask questions. And when something is changing, don't stop at acknowledging it. Have the awkward conversations about what care will require, who will provide it, how you'll pay for it, and how you'll show up for one another when things become more difficult. 

And please, don't stand on ceremony. Sometimes love requires a little less politeness and a lot more persistence.

Which brings me back to the Griswolds.

They never managed a perfect vacation or holiday, but boy, did they hang on tight. I loved helping cast that motley crew, and I suspect every actor brought a little of their own family lore to those gloriously ridiculous performances.

The thing about casting is that you spend a great deal of time looking for the right person for the right role. Of course, you can't cast your own family. You don't get to choose who shows up, who disappoints you, or who rises magnificently to the occasion. But you can ask people to pay closer attention and take on a bigger role. You can insist that the family gather around the table not simply to give thanks, but to really see one another.

And when it comes to caring for the people we love, I think we need to stop being so afraid of making a scene. 

After all, you may not be able to cast your own family. But you can demand a callback.

item.title: Connection Must Be More Than a Holiday Tradition
item.description: The connection that Thanksgiving creates should inspire us to address the loneliness epidemic, writes Suzanne McCormick.
item.content:encoded:
It’s Thanksgiving Day. For many of us, this means turkey and stuffing in the oven. Football playing in the background. Family and friends gathering to share a meal. And someone asking: “How about we go around and say what we’re thankful for?”

People share stories, discuss milestones, maybe even acknowledge personal challenges. And before it’s time for pumpkin pie, we’ve learned something new about one another and feel more connected than before.

Unfortunately, experiences of connection like this happen too infrequently. Today, loneliness and social isolation are among the most pressing public health challenges facing our country. According to a new Social Connection in America™ survey, 40% of Americans report moderate to severe loneliness. Nearly 70% get together with others no more than once or twice a month. While connecting virtually is a routine part of daily life for many, only 24% of people say it is as satisfying as spending time together in person.

As a leader at the YMCA, I spend a lot of time thinking about connection and community, and what happens when people don’t have either.

The consequences are real and extend beyond feeling down or lonely. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a lack of social connection is associated with an increased risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, dementia, earlier death, and other serious health conditions. In 2023, then-U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy warned that the nation’s epidemic of loneliness and isolation poses serious risks to both individual and public health.
These troubling trends and consequences coincide with a retreat from public life. A 2025 report from the Survey Center on American Life found that Americans began spending substantially less time in “third places” outside of the home and school or work—such as YMCAs, parks, and houses of worship—after the pandemic and still have not fully returned. 

A range of factors appear to be contributing to this decline, from the rise of remote work and the growing amount of time people are spending online, to stubbornly high inflation and the resulting increased cost of living. Americans are staying home more and going out and socializing less. When we spend less time in shared spaces, we lose natural opportunities to connect with others. Connection becomes something we have to intentionally seek out, rather than something woven throughout our day.

The good news is that spaces for connection are all around us. The challenge for each of us is to step into those spaces, open ourselves up to new relationships, and prioritize our intrinsic need for human connection.

In 1851, 175 years ago this December, the first YMCA was established in the United States. It was founded by Thomas Valentine Sullivan, a sea captain and missionary looking to provide a safe “home away from home” for sailors and merchants in need of community and support. As the needs of communities evolved, so did the Y. Our programs have changed and expanded over time, but creating places where people can find support and connection has remained central to our work.

Today, third spaces continue to provide that same community and support people need to thrive. They foster a deep sense of belonging and shared purpose—and often among people whose paths might not cross otherwise.

Over time, a familiar face turns into a friendship, a class becomes a community, and a third space feels like a second home. We know the ingredients for connection—programs that invite contribution, spaces that encourage conversation, staff trained to welcome—and how they fit together to create opportunities for growth, relationships, and belonging.

It can be hard to find the time, resources, or even courage to try something new, but the benefits of connection are worth it. This Thanksgiving, I hope we’ll all take time to appreciate the people around us. I hope we’ll listen a little more closely to their stories, share a little more of our own, and reflect on how meaningful it feels to truly connect with another person.

And I hope that after the dishes are cleared and everyone goes home, we’ll continue to make the effort. Because we need connection, and we need it to be more than a holiday tradition.
